extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, examiners, policymakers, and IP researchers interested in subject-matter/patent-eligibility issues
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and practical implications of the United States Supreme Court's Alice v. CLS Bank decision, which adopts the Mayo two‑step framework for determining patentable subject-matter (section 101) and discusses consequences for software, biotechnology, diagnostics, and business-method patents. Compares US approach to other jurisdictions and illustrates application with case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent must satisfy the requirement for patentable subject-matter (also called patent eligibility or the requirement for 'an invention'); the claimed invention must be the sort of thing that could lead to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most systems define subject-matter negatively (things are patentable unless excluded by statute or case law). Once subject-matter is satisfied, assessment turns to fact-specific criteria such as novelty, non-obviousness, industrial applicability, and sufficient description. If subject-matter is not satisfied, the application fails irrespective of those other considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized section 101 exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: US courts recognize three exclusions to patent-eligible subject-matter: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court links these exclusions to the principle of 'pre-emption' — preventing patents from monopolizing basic tools/building blocks of scientific and technological work which must remain in the public domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step test for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, consider the elements of each claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether the additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application — i.e., whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the uniform subject-matter test the Supreme Court endorsed in Alice, generalized from Mayo. Evaluate both individual claim elements and their ordered combination; search for an 'inventive concept.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify 'abstract ideas' by example
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas include, per the Court's examples, fundamental economic practices; certain methods of organizing human activities; an idea in itself; and mathematical relationships/formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court did not attempt to delimit the precise contours of 'abstract ideas', but provided these illustrative categories to guide Step 1 analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation does not salvage an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely requiring generic computer implementation — e.g., adding 'apply it' with a generic computer and generic computer functions — fails to transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice Court explicitly held that claims drawn to intermediated settlement that merely required a data processing system, communications controller, and data storage unit (generic computer components) were ineligible. Claim drafters must do more than append conventional computing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer functioning or other technology is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that improve the functioning of a computer itself (speed, efficiency, security), or effect an improvement in any other technology or technical field, are patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice recognized longstanding precedent (1970s/80s) that such technological improvements stand apart from abstract ideas. Emphasizes that solving a technological problem or improving a technical process supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diehr principle — using an otherwise unpatentable equation to solve a technological problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Diamond v. Diehr supports patentability where an otherwise unpatentable equation is used to 'solve a technological problem' and 'improve an existing technological process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice opinion characterizes Diehr as patentable for that reason, suggesting claims that integrate mathematical formulas into technological solutions can be eligible if they produce a practical technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical algorithms/manipulation of data without physical device are suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: A process that employs mathematical algorithms to manipulate existing information to generate additional information may be patent-ineligible if it recites an ineligible abstract process of gathering and combining data and does not require input from a physical device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As illustrated by Digitech v. Electronics for Imaging, such claims are likely to fail Step 2 unless they include additional limitations that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea/algorithm itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-emption as the underlying policy test
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle underlying the exclusions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) is pre-emption: patents should not 'swallow' basic tools of innovation by monopolizing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing eligibility, consider whether the claim would pre-empt use of the basic idea or tool across fields; prevention of pre-emption supports exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim analysis: individual elements and ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be evaluated both element-by-element and as an ordered combination to determine whether the claim transforms an ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step Two explicitly requires this two-pronged claim analysis; inventive concept may arise from the arrangement/combination of elements even if individual elements are conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and vagueness of terms like 'technological' and 'inventive concept'
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used in the Alice decision—such as 'generic', 'technological', 'inventive concept', and the transformation into 'something more'—are undefined, vague, and will be heavily litigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: these imprecise labels can create tortuous analyses and subjective decisions; the tests can overlap with novelty and inventive-step considerations and may produce inconsistent outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter criterion is a coarse, preliminary filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter eligibility serves as a coarse filter that can prematurely eliminate patents based on limited information and may overlap with novelty and inventive step determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying too heavily on subject-matter rejections can deprive the patent system of substantive fact-based comparisons against prior art; it is an impressionistic and sometimes inefficient tool for weeding out weak patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variance in applying subject-matter rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Different jurisdictions apply the subject-matter requirement differently: e.g., the UK courts treat subject-matter as a real threshold and use complicated tests, whereas the European Patent Office sets a lower bar for subject-matter and addresses exclusions (software, business methods) at novelty/non-obviousness stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and practitioners should tailor drafting and argument strategies to local practice: what fails under US Alice/Mayo reasoning might be approached differently at the EPO or UK courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting implication: integrate building blocks into 'something more'
rubrics_metrics.description: To pass the two-step test, claims should integrate otherwise unpatentable building blocks (abstract ideas, laws of nature) into an inventive application — 'something more' — rather than claiming the building block itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to show how the claimed elements combine to produce a technical effect, solution to a technological problem, or a meaningful improvement in computer or other technology; avoid purely abstract formulations with only conventional implementation steps.
